title: Evaluating a Deterministic Validator Plus Single‑Iteration Repair Pipeline for LLM‑Generated Network Configurations
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment (cand-2026-001-A-prereg-v1) to measure whether a minimal guarded pipeline—single‑shot LLM generation (declared model: gpt-5-mini) followed by a frozen deterministic configuration validator and at most one automated repair iteration—reduces first‑pass misconfiguration relative to plain single‑shot generation on a fixed set of intent→configuration tasks. We ran N=300 paired tasks (600 episodes) using 301 model calls (300 shared initial generations + 1 repair). Observed outcomes: baseline valid = 299/300 (99.667%); guarded valid = 300/300 (100.0%); paired counts n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; absolute paired difference = 0.0033333; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). The single allowed automated repair corrected the sole invalid baseline output (repair success 1/1; Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]). The observed near‑ceiling baseline contradicted the preregistered planning assumption (planned baseline pass rate = 0.40), eliminating statistical headroom for the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction target. We report preregistered design elements, exact artifact‑derived counts, inferential results, an artifact‑grounded post‑hoc sensitivity bound, and concrete design recommendations for future NetOps confirmatory evaluations. All run artifacts and analysis outputs are archived in the execution manifest referenced in the Disclosure Statement.

sections.introduction: Translating operator intent into device configuration is central to NetOps. Probabilistic LLM generation promises productivity gains but risks unsafe or incorrect changes (misordering, omission, unsafe commands). Prior work advocates hybrid generate→verify→repair designs pairing LLMs with deterministic validators or simulators to mitigate risk. We evaluate a narrowly scoped operational question: under paired shared‑candidate semantics, can a frozen deterministic validator plus a single automated repair iteration reduce first‑pass misconfiguration relative to the unguarded single‑shot generator? Our contributions: (1) a preregistered paired experiment with deterministic task seeds and archived per‑task artifacts, (2) artifact‑grounded confirmatory statistics, (3) a post‑hoc sensitivity bound tied to observed discordant counts, and (4) artifact‑traceable recommendations for future NetOps confirmatory designs.
sections.related_work: Recent demonstrations show LLMs can synthesize network configuration templates in lab settings but report operational failure modes (misordering, omission, overconfidence) [10.1002/nem.2313]. Work in adjacent domains documents that verifier‑assisted or retrieval‑augmented pipelines reduce factual errors and improve grounding, motivating guarded architectures for NetOps [10.36227/techrxiv.176784505.56675782/v1, 10.2139/ssrn.6608518]. Classic deterministic verification approaches (e.g., header‑space and specification checking) provide algorithmic foundations for static validators that can check reachability and policy constraints without live execution [10.1145/3098822.3098834]. Surveys highlight auditability and oversight concerns for agentic NetOps workflows [10.6028/nist.ai.100-2e2023]. Our experiment positions a preregistered confirmatory test within this body of work by measuring first‑pass validity under a bounded repair budget and shared‑candidate pairing.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and design: The study was preregistered (cand-2026-001-A-prereg-v1) and executed under adapter hosted_netops_gvr_v1 with a frozen validator/repair adapter deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Sampling: paired within‑task design with 300 deterministic seeds producing paired episodes (600 episodes total). Shared_initial_candidate semantics were preregistered: the same single generated candidate per task served as the baseline response and the starting point for validation and possible repair in the guarded arm. Model and calls: declared generation model = gpt-5-mini; execution used a planned maximum of 600 model calls and adhered to the preregistered single‑retry policy for infrastructure failures. The archived execution/model_configuration.json records declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini" and "temperature": null (artifact path: execution/model_configuration.json; SHA-256: 1acce92558edeb13cd97b75817329d332afe4a36d01d566f1a26c61b132923fa). A null/unset temperature in the recorded artifact is not evidence of deterministic sampling (temperature=0); sampling determinism was therefore unspecified by the recorded configuration and could affect generator variance across independent draws. Validator and repair behavior: the deterministic validator canonicalized configurations to a normalized AST and applied full intent‑constraint checks (required_sequence, expected_final_state, workflow policies). The repair adapter was invoked only when the validator reported violations and was bounded to a single automated repair attempt per episode. Primary estimand and test: preregistered primary estimand = paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline; primary test = exact McNemar two‑sided (α=0.05) with paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). Power planning: the preregistration used a planning baseline pass rate = 0.40 to set sample size; we report this planning assumption because the observed baseline diverged and it materially affects inferential interpretation.
sections.results: Execution accounting (artifact‑derived): run started 2026-08-30T13:23:48.902902+00:00 and completed 2026-08-30T14:03:29.033723+00:00. Planned episodes = 600; completed = 600; complete analyzed pairs = 300. Model_calls_used = 301 (300 shared initial generations + 1 repair). No provider/infrastructure failures occurred. Primary outcomes (archived counts): Baseline_success_count = 299/300 (99.667%); Guarded_success_count = 300/300 (100.0%). Paired contingency derived from archived artifacts: n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0. Inferential results (preregistered): exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; absolute paired difference = 0.0033333; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). Repair outcomes (H2): the single allowed automated repair corrected the sole invalid baseline output (repair success 1/1; Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]). Post‑hoc sensitivity bound: with total discordant pairs = 1, the maximal resolvable absolute paired difference equals 1/300 ≈ 0.00333, explaining why the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction (planned under baseline=0.40) could not be detected given the observed near‑ceiling baseline. All counts and intervals are reproducible from the archived execution and analysis artifacts.
sections.discussion: Artifact‑grounded interpretation: the archived contingency (n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0) constrains inference—paired difference = (n10 − n01)/N = 1/300 ≈ 0.00333 and the exact McNemar test conditions on the observed discordant count, yielding p = 1.00. Design tradeoffs: shared_initial_candidate pairing improves ecological validity for studying remediation of a single plan but increases within‑pair correlation and reduces informative discordant pairs, lowering McNemar power for large preregistered effects. Practical recommendations (artifact‑traceable): (1) calibrate task difficulty or adversarially augment the task bank to ensure a nontrivial baseline failure prevalence or a preregistered discordant‑pair target aligned with the planned absolute/relative effect size; (2) explicitly preregister pairing semantics and repair budgets and incorporate them into power/sample‑size computations; (3) when runtime semantics matter, integrate emulation/simulation stages and preregister how emulator outcomes map to success/failure. Validator traces (normalized_configuration, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation_codes, repair_applied) proved essential for diagnosis and reproducible post‑mortems; per‑task structured traces are a recommended archival practice. Construct‑validity caveat: our validator performs static deterministic checks rather than dynamic emulation, so runtime control‑plane or dataplane dynamics were not measured. Thus, operational claims about runtime consequences require emulation integration in future runs.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired experiment (N=300 pairs) comparing single‑shot LLM generation (gpt-5-mini) to a guarded pipeline of frozen deterministic validation plus a single automated repair iteration. Observed results: baseline 299/300 valid, guarded 300/300 valid; single repair corrected the only invalid baseline output. The observed near‑ceiling baseline contradicted the preregistered planning assumption (baseline=0.40), eliminating statistical headroom to detect the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction. Future confirmatory NetOps evaluations should align task difficulty or adversarial augmentation with planned estimand precision, explicitly preregister pairing semantics and repair budgets, and add emulation when runtime semantics are operationally relevant. All raw responses, validator traces, repair traces, execution manifest, and analysis artifacts are archived and are the authoritative source for the reported counts and intervals.

limitations: Synthetic task bank and constrained vendor‑template scope limit external validity to broad production environments.
Single LLM (gpt-5-mini) and a single validator implementation restrict generality across model families and validator designs.

The preregistered power plan assumed a baseline pass rate = 0.40; the observed baseline (299/300) contradicted that assumption and removed headroom to detect the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction.
Sampling semantics (shared_initial_candidate) reused the same initial candidate across paired arms, increasing within‑pair correlation and reducing discordant pairs available to McNemar inference.

Validation used deterministic static configuration/constraint checks rather than full dynamic emulation of runtime semantic effects; actual runtime consequences of configurations were not executed and remain unmeasured.

H2 repair‑success evidence is based on a single initially invalid case (1/1 → 100%), yielding a wide Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]; larger counts of initial failures are required to estimate repair effectiveness precisely.
